analysis.one_liner: Raises estate taxes on the largest fortunes to 65% and closes trust loopholes, leaving 99.5% of estates untouched.
analysis.headline: Sanders' bill to raise estate taxes on the largest fortunes and close trust loopholes sat in the Senate Finance Committee for 21 months and never got a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise taxes on the very largest inheritances: it cuts the untaxed estate threshold to $3.5 million, raises the top rate on billion-dollar estates to 65%, and shuts down a series of trust and valuation tricks that wealthy families use to shrink their taxable estates. At the same time, it expands protections for family farms and land donated for conservation. The 99.5% of estates that fall below the new threshold would pay nothing under it.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, families leaving estates below $3.5 million would owe nothing (the tax would not touch 99.5% of estates). Farmers and landowners would gain bigger estate-tax breaks: the farm-valuation reduction rises from $750,000 to $3 million and the conservation-easement exclusion rises from $500,000 to $2 million. The general public would gain revenue collected from the largest fortunes and fewer loopholes.

how_it_helps.text: The tax would apply only to the largest estates: the basic exclusion is set at $3.5 million, and rates of 45%, 50%, 55%, and 65% would apply only above that level, with the 65% rate kicking in above $1 billion.
Farm families get more room to pass land on: the reduction in farmland value for estate tax purposes quadruples from $750,000 to $3 million, adjusted for inflation.
Landowners who donate conservation easements get a bigger break: the exclusion rises from $500,000 to $2 million and the applicable percentage from 40% to 60%.

The bill closes loopholes used mainly by very wealthy families, including eliminating the step-up in basis for property in grantor trusts, requiring minimum 10-year terms and minimum remainder values for GRATs, taxing sales between a grantor and the grantor's own trust, denying valuation discounts on nonbusiness assets held in family entities, and ending the generation-skipping exemption for trusts designed to last indefinitely.
Executors and gift-tax filers would have to disclose the value of each interest received to the Treasury and to recipients, improving reporting of large transfers.

analysis.who_pays: If passed, the cost would fall on heirs of estates worth more than $3.5 million, with the steepest rates — up to 65% — on estates over $1 billion. Wealthy families using grantor trusts, GRATs, and long-duration dynasty trusts to avoid the tax would also pay more. Estate planners and tax lawyers advising these clients would lose business.

drawbacks.text: Closing valuation discounts and tightening GRAT and grantor-trust rules would also raise compliance costs for some legitimate small-business and family partnerships, not just for billionaires' avoidance schemes.

A 65% rate on billion-dollar estates and a $3.5 million exemption would be among the highest combined estate-tax burdens in the developed world, and critics argue such rates push wealth out of productive investment or into avoidance.

The lower $3.5 million exemption and the new per-donor cap on gifts into trusts would raise the tax for some families well short of the ultra-wealthy tier, particularly in high-cost regions with expensive homes and land.
Collecting from the largest estates depends on valuation and enforcement work by the Treasury Department, which the bill does not fund or staff.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains and costs are unevenly distributed by design. Ordinary taxpayers would see no change at all — the bill exempts 99.5% of estates — while farms and conservation donors would actually get larger breaks than they have now. The entire cost concentrates on heirs of the largest 0.5% of estates and on the professionals who help them avoid the tax. The main honest criticisms are the design details: the new anti-avoidance rules are complex and would sweep in some ordinary family businesses, and a 65% top rate invites avoidance and enforcement battles. Weighing that against the scale of untaxed dynastic wealth the bill targets, the benefits to the general public outweigh the costs, but the bill never got far enough for that tradeoff to be debated on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: Sanders introduced the bill and it was sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sanders introduced the bill on March 25, 2021 with four Democratic cosponsors: Gillibrand, Whitehouse, Van Hollen, and Reed.
The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the full action record shows no hearing, no markup, and no vote ever took place.
The bill died at the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023 without ever reaching the Senate floor.

The estate tax provisions the bill would have changed — the 40% top rate and the roughly $12 million exemption — remained in force, leaving the largest estates taxed as they were before the bill was filed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The wealthiest families and the estate-planning industry came out ahead: the current estate tax — a 40% top rate with an exemption of roughly $12 million per person — stayed in place, and the trust and valuation strategies the bill targeted remained fully available.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the For the 99.5 Percent Act on March 25, 2021.

for.name: 5 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill alongside the sponsor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Senate Finance Committee (Chair: Ron Wyden, D-RI)
against.what_they_did: The Finance Committee, chaired by Sen. Wyden, never held a markup or vote on the bill; after being referred on March 25, 2021, it saw no further action.

against.name: 50 of 50 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican supported the bill, and a Senate in which the opposing caucus held 50 seats would have needed 60 votes to advance any major tax bill; no movement occurred.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's only support came from Sen. Sanders and five Democratic cosponsors, with no Republicans signing on.

industries.industry: Estate planning and wealth management (trust attorneys, advisors, GRAT and dynasty-trust services)
industries.note: The bill's core changes — closing grantor trust, GRAT, and valuation-discount strategies — would shrink demand for elaborate estate-tax avoidance planning. The industry's interest in preserving these strategies runs against ordinary taxpayers, who pay for avoided tax through lost revenue or higher rates elsewhere.

The bill quadruples the special farm-valuation reduction from $750,000 to $3 million and indexes it to inflation, and nearly quadruples the conservation-easement exclusion, so farms and ranches would face less estate tax pressure than under current law even as large estates generally pay more.

industries.industry: Ultra-wealthy families (estates over $3.5 million, especially over $1 billion)
industries.note: The bill caps minority-interest and lack-of-marketability discounts and limits the generation-skipping exemption to trusts ending within 50 years, making the most common dynasty-wealth structures less useful. This affects very few families, but the revenue foregone under current rules falls on everyone else.
